domain_assessment.domain: Manufacturing production planning and control in a metal-stamping operation
domain_assessment.role: PPC analyst responsible for a rolling five-day schedule across three presses and coordination with three downstream assembly plants
domain_assessment.objective: Maintain production continuity and on-time shipments while responding to increased demand, a coil-steel supply delay, and emerging equipment-reliability risk on a constrained press
domain_assessment.incident_type: Concurrent production-scheduling, supplier-delay, and machinery-reliability disruption involving Press 3

decision_points.summary: Monday allocation decision: assign the entire incremental bracket batch to Press 3 despite a brief low-priority vibration-advisory flag.
evidence_before: Weekend demand surge for a high-volume bracket variant
Press 3 was the only press currently tooled for the part
Prior-week throughput report showing Press 3 ran above target
Brief scheduling-assistant flag that Press 3 had an open vibration advisory
The full CMMS entry was available but was not reviewed
evidence_after: Maintenance technician later mentioned a recommended follow-up inspection within two weeks
The participant later stated that a full dashboard entry might have caused them to pause longer
goals_constraints: Meet the assembly plant's incremental demand
Avoid Press 1 retooling and its associated changeover cost
Use the only currently tooled press
alternatives: Allocate the full extra batch to Press 3
Split the batch between Press 3 and a temporarily retooled Press 1
Push part of the batch to the following week
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant explicitly treated recent, concrete throughput evidence as more probative than a vague low-priority vibration flag.
decision_points.time_pressure: Moderate to high because of the demand surge and schedule implications, although the interview does not establish an immediate deadline that made CMMS review impossible.
decision_points.uncertainty: Whether strong recent throughput was an adequate indicator of additional safe loading when a maintenance-related vibration concern was also known.

decision_points.summary: Tuesday supplier-response decision: predict that a four-day coil-steel delay would resolve like prior supplier delays and contact the first familiar backup supplier without comparing alternatives.
evidence_before: Supplier representative reported a four-day delay
Participant recalled two earlier supplier delays, around late December and late June, that resolved within a week
Participant had a pre-existing relationship with one backup supplier
evidence_after: No comparative assessment of backup suppliers' lead times or prices was performed
The participant retained the familiar supplier as a reserve option rather than immediately ordering backup stock
goals_constraints: Respond while already managing several simultaneous operational demands
alternatives: Contact the known backup supplier as a reserve
Compare multiple backup suppliers before selecting one
Wait for the primary supplier's delay to resolve
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant elevated a perceived recurring timing pattern over the supplier's stated current cause and selected a familiar acceptable sourcing option under time and attention constraints.
decision_points.time_pressure: High; the participant reports that the operation was already stretched and that there was no clean window for comparison shopping.
decision_points.uncertainty: Whether the current allocation-constraint explanation reflected the same mechanism, duration, and operational risk as prior delays.

decision_points.summary: Thursday information-seeking decision: decline to review a full three-week vibration trend log after learning that Press 3 vibration had increased slightly.
evidence_before: Reliability engineer reported a slight increase in vibration since the weekend run
A full three-week vibration trend log was available
Participant recalled a vivid past Press 1 fire as the salient reference case for serious press failure
The bi-weekly maintenance review was approaching
evidence_after: The trend log was not reviewed
The participant later acknowledged that the full log could have shown a clearer upward trend and might have forced reworking Friday's plan
Engineering escalated the status to "elevated concern" on Friday
goals_constraints: Determine whether emerging reliability information warranted schedule intervention
Avoid operational disruption during an already overloaded week
Maintain a confirmed production plan unless new evidence justified change
alternatives: Review the full vibration trend log immediately
Seek additional clarification from reliability engineering
Wait for the bi-weekly maintenance review
Treat the single vibration update as insufficiently urgent for further inquiry
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant regarded the single update as non-dramatic, judged risk against a vivid remembered fire, and chose not to expose themselves to trend information that might require a difficult reschedule.
decision_points.time_pressure: Present and operationally relevant, but not so absolute that information review was impossible.
decision_points.uncertainty: Whether the slight increase represented an isolated non-critical variation or part of a worsening three-week reliability trend.

decision_points.summary: Friday schedule-commitment decision: retain most of the Press 3 plan after engineering upgraded the status to "elevated concern," while making only a slight reduction in loading.
evidence_before: Engineering changed Press 3's status from "monitor" to "elevated concern"
The engineer clarified that the change reflected a real increase in loading risk rather than a purely administrative status change
Downstream plants had already received schedule confirmation
Shifting remaining volume to Press 1 would require several hours of partial changeover
The participant retained confidence in prior throughput data and the clean weekend run
evidence_after: The Friday run was trimmed slightly but not substantially reallocated
Press 3 completed the week without failure
Reliability formally recommended reduced loading for the following cycle
goals_constraints: Avoid disruption to downstream plant commitments
Respond to elevated reliability risk without unnecessarily destabilizing the schedule
alternatives: Reallocate more volume to Press 1 despite the changeover cost
Defer or delay a portion of the scheduled work
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant explicitly gave greater weight to prior throughput and weekend-run evidence than to the clarified elevated-concern risk signal.
decision_points.time_pressure: High because the weekly schedule was being finalized and downstream plants had already been confirmed.
decision_points.uncertainty: The precise probability and timing of downtime remained unspecified, but engineering had clarified that loading risk had materially increased.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “The flag was there, but it was low-priority and vague next to a full week of solid output numbers, so the throughput report just carried more weight for me.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Monday allocation follow-up after the interviewer asks why the throughput report was decisive despite the vibration flag.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant had both favorable throughput evidence and a potentially disconfirming vibration-advisory flag before finalizing allocation. They explicitly weighted the evidence supporting the preferred Press 3 capacity conclusion more heavily and treated the contrary reliability signal as insufficiently meaningful to alter the decision.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The vibration flag was described as low-priority and vague, while the throughput report was recent and concrete. A scheduler could reasonably give the detailed output data greater weight if the advisory did not indicate material loading risk.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is needed for the intended occurrence. The text now makes both evidence sources cognitively available and makes the participant's relative weighting explicit.

revision.location: Decision point 1, Monday allocation chronology and the throughput-evidence probe.
revision.current_defect: None material for the requested confirmation-bias occurrence.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the brief pre-allocation advisory flag, the recent throughput report, and the participant's explicit statement that throughput carried more weight. Do not add a stronger maintenance warning, because that would make the decision implausibly reckless rather than subtly selective.
preserve: Low-priority and abbreviated nature of the advisory flag
The participant's access to a full CMMS entry only through additional effort
The counterfactual focus on advisory presentation in the scheduling workflow
avoid_creating: A separate Ostrich-effect occurrence at decision point 1
A duplicate conservatism-bias occurrence before Friday

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I didn't compare lead times or pricing against other options that morning — there wasn't a clean window to do that kind of comparison shopping with everything else going on.”
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: Under limited time and attention, the participant selected the first familiar, acceptable backup-supplier contact rather than generating and comparatively evaluating alternatives. This is a satisficing alternative-selection process.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Calling a known supplier first can be a rational operational shortcut when the supplier is qualified, time is scarce, and the participant only seeks a reserve option rather than an immediate purchase commitment.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is required. The episode is sufficiently distinct from the supplier-delay causal-attribution episode.

revision.current_defect: None material. The interview identifies constrained search, an available familiar option, and lack of comparative evaluation.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the existing response and its distinction from the participant's inference about the primary supplier delay.
preserve: The pre-existing relationship with the backup supplier
No comparison of lead times or pricing
The backup supplier as a reserve rather than an immediate procurement commitment
avoid_creating: An assertion that the familiar supplier was known to be inferior
Merging this alternative-selection mechanism with the temporal causal-attribution mechanism

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Their delays always seem to cluster around certain stretches for them, so I read the timing itself as the real signal — the ‘internal allocation constraints’ line sounded like their usual wording, not something new.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Tuesday supplier-delay chronology; reinforced in the follow-up explaining why backup stock was not ordered immediately.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant infers that the current delay arises from a recurring time-based pattern and discounts the supplier's stated present cause. The participant treats superficial timing similarity across two earlier delays as evidence of the causal explanation for the current event, rather than merely as a limited predictive prior.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The same supplier's prior delay history could be diagnostically useful if the participant had reliable knowledge that delays recur seasonally. However, the interview supplies only two loosely timed prior events and no operational evidence tying them to a common seasonal mechanism, while the current supplier gives a potentially distinct allocation-based explanation.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is needed for the specified temporal-pattern causal-attribution occurrence. The current wording makes the participant's causal interpretation and discounting of contrary explanation observable.

revision.current_defect: None material after revision. The text now contains an explicit timing-based causal inference rather than only a similarity-based forecast.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the participant's statement that timing was treated as the real signal and that the stated allocation constraint was discounted as routine wording.
preserve: The supplier representative's stated internal-allocation explanation
avoid_creating: A stronger unsupported claim that the participant had proof of seasonality
A second representativeness or availability episode framed as a separate occurrence
A causal explanation based on vendor trust rather than temporal pattern matching

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Even with the engineer telling me it reflected a real risk increase, the earlier data — the throughput numbers, the clean weekend run — still felt like the more solid read on how Press 3 actually performs, so I didn't weight the new label as heavily as what I already had.”
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant receives a clarified new engineering assessment indicating a real increase in loading risk, but explicitly gives less weight to that new evidence than to the prior throughput-based reliability belief. The transcript identifies under-updating rather than merely schedule lock-in because the participant directly states the relative evidentiary weighting.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Confirmed downstream schedules and several hours of changeover are genuine operational costs, and the engineer did not provide a quantified downtime probability. The participant's slight run reduction also shows some updating rather than total disregard.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is required. The explicit statement that the new risk signal was weighted less heavily than prior evidence supports the requested belief-updating mechanism.

revision.current_defect: None material. Legitimate operational constraints remain present, but the participant's expressed evidence weighting independently identifies the intended mechanism.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the engineer's clarification of a real loading-risk increase and the participant's explicit statement that earlier evidence received more weight.
preserve: The slight reduction in Friday loading
The distinction between Monday allocation-stage evidence weighting and Friday belief updating
avoid_creating: An additional status-quo or sunk-cost episode that displaces the intended conservatism mechanism
A categorical refusal to act on engineering advice

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “I was thinking of the Press 1 fire from a couple years ago — that's the reference point that comes to mind when someone says ‘press failure.’ This didn't look anything like that, so it didn't register as urgent.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Thursday probe asking what situation the participant pictured when assessing seriousness.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant judges current vibration risk against an easily recalled, dramatic, catastrophic fire. Because the current gradual signal lacks the vivid features of that remembered incident, the participant experiences it as less urgent despite an available source of more directly relevant trend evidence.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Experienced operators may use major past incidents as useful comparative references. Here, however, the participant explicitly identifies the vivid incident as the reference point that caused the current gradual signal not to register as urgent, supporting the memory-vividness mechanism.

revision.location: Decision point 3, remembered-incident probe and response.
revision.current_defect: None material. The recalled event, its salience, and its effect on risk judgment are explicit.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the current wording. It should remain a memory-based severity judgment and not be rewritten as a refusal to inspect evidence.
preserve: The contrast between catastrophic failure and gradual vibration change
avoid_creating: A duplicate imaginability cue at a different decision point
Merging this instance with the trend-log avoidance episode
An unrealistic claim that only catastrophic events justify maintenance action

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: “Pulling three weeks of data might have shown a clearer upward line than a single number did, and that could have meant reworking Friday's plan on top of everything else already moving. The bi-weekly review was close enough that it felt fine to let it sit until then.”
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Thursday trend-log probe, including the interviewer's question about whether opening the log would have changed required action that day.
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant acknowledges that the available trend log could reveal a worsening pattern and trigger an inconvenient schedule revision, then elects not to inspect it immediately. This is information avoidance directed at potentially decision-forcing risk information, not simply absence of information or ordinary inability to access it.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Deferring review to an imminent scheduled maintenance meeting may be a reasonable triage decision if the new signal is mild and no immediate threshold has been crossed. The avoidance interpretation is nevertheless supported because the participant links non-review to the possibility that the information would necessitate reworking Friday's plan.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: No additional evidence is required. The transcript now identifies the available information, the anticipated unfavorable implication of learning it, and the choice to defer review.

revision.location: Decision point 3, trend-log review probe and response.
revision.current_defect: None material. The information-avoidance mechanism is now independently observable.
revision.minimal_change_instruction: Retain the current response linking possible discovery of an upward trend to the prospect of reworking Friday's schedule.
preserve: The separate vivid-memory mechanism for imaginability bias
avoid_creating: A duplicate conservatism-bias episode on Thursday
A statement that the participant deliberately violated a mandatory reliability review procedure
An explicit self-labeling statement such as "I avoided the information"

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “At that point we were locked in with the downstream plants, and a full reallocation meant hours of changeover we didn't have room for.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The existing confirmed schedule may have gained psychological weight because changing it would impose disruption and coordination costs.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The transcript identifies concrete switching costs, downstream commitments, and a limited amount of remaining schedule flexibility. These may fully explain retention of the plan without invoking a preference for the status quo.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “That's the reference point that comes to mind when someone says ‘press failure.’”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The vivid prior fire is readily retrieved and becomes the dominant comparator in the participant's risk assessment.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: This is substantively overlapping with the intended Imaginability Bias rather than a separate distinct occurrence. It should not be separately counted unless the annotation taxonomy intentionally differentiates availability and imaginability.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: “The earlier data — the throughput numbers, the clean weekend run — still felt like the more solid read on how Press 3 actually performs.”
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: Earlier throughput and weekend-run evidence may serve as an anchor against which the later reliability escalation is insufficiently adjusted.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The mechanism is already adequately represented by the requested Conservatism Bias occurrence and should not be counted as an accidental additional instance.

nonbias_cues.cue: Press 3 completed the week without failing, and shipments went out on time.
nonbias_cues.location: Outcome question near the end of the interview.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The outcome does not establish whether earlier reasoning was biased or unbiased. A biased process can produce a favorable result, and a sound process can still produce a failure.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant chose a known backup supplier quickly.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Speed and use of an existing relationship alone are not bias. The bounded-rationality occurrence is supported only because the participant explicitly reports constrained search and no comparative evaluation of otherwise available alternatives.

nonbias_cues.cue: The vibration advisory was low-priority and abbreviated.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: A vague low-priority advisory could reasonably receive less weight than detailed recent throughput information. The occurrence is annotated as confirmation bias because the participant explicitly describes relative weighting of favorable and potentially disconfirming evidence, not because the advisory necessarily should have been dispositive.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant faced confirmed downstream schedules and a multi-hour partial changeover.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: These are genuine operational constraints. They do not independently prove conservatism bias; the target occurrence is supported by the separate explicit statement that the new clarified risk information was weighted less heavily than earlier evidence.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant waited for the bi-weekly maintenance review.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Deferral to an imminent formal review can be legitimate risk triage. The Ostrich-effect occurrence is supported not by deferral alone, but by the participant's stated concern that reviewing the full log could reveal a trend requiring a difficult schedule rework.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant had prior experience with supplier delays from the same supplier.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Past vendor performance is a potentially valid input. The correlation-bias occurrence depends on the stronger statement that timing itself was treated as the causal signal and the stated present allocation constraint was dismissed as routine wording.

causal_claims.claim: The participant infers that the timing of prior supplier delays explains the current supplier delay more reliably than the supplier's stated internal-allocation constraint.
causal_claims.assessment: The interview now clearly contains a causal attribution based on superficial temporal pattern matching. The evidence is weak for the actual causal conclusion because it relies on only two prior events, uses broad timing categories, and does not establish a common mechanism.

causal_claims.claim: A clearer upward vibration trend could have required reworking Friday's schedule.
causal_claims.assessment: This is a plausible operational conditional claim. The interview does not quantify the engineering threshold or probability of downtime, but it sufficiently establishes the participant's anticipated consequence of learning adverse trend information.

causal_claims.claim: The Friday elevated-concern designation reflected a real increase in loading risk.
causal_claims.assessment: The engineer's clarification is presented as new expert evidence. It supports the conservatism-bias mechanism because the participant explicitly discounts it relative to the earlier favorable evidence; it does not itself establish an exact downtime probability.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: The participant treats the timing of two previous delays as the real explanatory signal and discounts the current allocation-based explanation.
correlation_causation_risks.implication: This supports the intended correlation-bias occurrence but remains a weak substantive causal inference because correlation in timing does not establish a recurring causal process.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: The successful end-of-week outcome could be interpreted retrospectively as confirming the supplier-delay and Press 3 reliability judgments.
correlation_causation_risks.implication: The outcome must not be used to validate the participant's earlier causal inferences, evidence weights, or information-avoidance decision.

causal_audit.changed_variable: The presentation of the Press 3 maintenance advisory at the Monday allocation point, from a brief scheduling-assistant flag with full detail available only through additional lookup to a full entry directly visible on the scheduling dashboard.
held_constant: Weekend demand surge and required batch size
Press 3 tooling exclusivity for the bracket variant
Supplier delay timing and stated cause
causal_audit.explanation: The participant-level counterfactual is coherent in the limited sense that more visible and detailed maintenance information is predicted to cause greater pause and reconsideration at allocation. However, it does not perfectly preserve the hidden specification's single manipulated variable. The revised interview changes both presentation channel and information detail: the original condition includes a brief pre-allocation flag, while the counterfactual introduces a full dashboard entry. The hidden specification describes the original state as CMMS-only and the changed state as prominent dashboard visibility. Therefore, the current counterfactual mixes visibility, workflow integration, and richness of maintenance information, reducing causal isolation.

global_revision_constraints: All six requested bias occurrences are now independently supported and should remain intact.
Preserve exactly four decision points and the existing chronological sequence.
Do not use the favorable operational outcome as evidence that any earlier reasoning process was sound.
Keep decision point 2 divided into a timing-based causal attribution episode and a separate backup-supplier alternative-selection episode.
Keep decision point 3 divided into a vivid-memory risk-judgment episode and a separate avoidance-of-decision-forcing-information episode.
Do not make the maintenance advisory more severe, mandatory, or explicit than necessary; doing so would reduce subtlety and create implausible behavior.
Do not introduce a second causal change in the counterfactual while repairing counterfactual fidelity.
revision_order: Revise only the counterfactual framing or the corresponding hidden counterfactual specification so that the manipulated variable is singular and precisely named.
After the counterfactual repair, confirm that the Monday confirmation-bias occurrence still retains pre-decision awareness of the advisory and explicit relative evidence weighting.
Do not revise the six target-bias passages unless the counterfactual repair inadvertently changes their evidence structure.

failure_flags.description: The current interview changes more than advisory visibility in its counterfactual. It contrasts a brief scheduling-side flag with a full dashboard entry, confounding visibility/workflow integration with the amount and specificity of maintenance information.

The hidden specification states that the original advisory was logged only in CMMS, whereas the interview states that the participant received a brief scheduling-assistant flag before allocation. This revision successfully supports confirmation bias but no longer exactly matches the stated original counterfactual baseline.
